name: Oleocanthal
description: Phenolic compound in EVOO that inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes — the same targets as ibuprofen — producing anti-inflammatory effects

name: Hydroxytyrosol
description: Potent antioxidant polyphenol in EVOO; scavenges free radicals and reduces LDL oxidation

name: Oleic acid
description: Monounsaturated fatty acid (>70% of EVOO); promotes reverse cholesterol transport and reduces vascular inflammation

name: Oleuropein
description: Polyphenol precursor abundant in Cretan EVOO; anti-inflammatory and cardioprotective effects

name: Apigenin
description: Flavone abundant in Sideritis scardica; anti-inflammatory (COX inhibition) comparable to indomethacin in animal models; gastroprotective

name: Luteolin
description: Flavone in Sideritis scardica; anti-inflammatory and antioxidant; synergistic effects with apigenin

name: Verbascoside (acteoside)
description: Phenylpropanoid glycoside in Sideritis; binds NLRP3 inflammasome (Kd 0.67 μM) and NF-κB (Kd 0.01 μM); key mechanistic driver of anti-inflammatory activity

name: Hydroxy-cinnamic acids
description: Class of phenolic acids in Sideritis (includes rosmarinic acid); implicated in monoamine reuptake inhibition and cerebral blood flow increase underlying cognitive effects

name: Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA)
description: Plant-derived omega-3 fatty acid; purslane is the richest known leafy vegetable source; anti-inflammatory precursor to EPA and DHA; lowers LDL and triglycerides

name: Portulacaxanthin
description: Yellow betalain pigment unique to purslane; potent antioxidant; scavenges free radicals and reduces oxidative stress markers

name: Kaempferol
description: Flavonol polyphenol in purslane; inhibits pro-inflammatory cytokines including TNF-α and IL-6; contributes to joint and vascular anti-inflammatory effects

name: Purslane mucilage polysaccharides
description: Gel-forming soluble fibre in purslane; acts as a prebiotic and bulk-forming agent; supports gut motility and colonic transit time reduction

name: Vitamin K2 (menaquinone)
description: Produced during fermentation of aged hard cheese; activates matrix Gla-protein which prevents calcium from depositing in artery walls; may explain cheese's paradoxical cardiovascular protection despite saturated fat content

name: Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)
description: Natural trans-fatty acid found at higher concentrations in sheep and goat dairy from pasture-fed animals; anti-inflammatory and potentially antiatherogenic

name: ACE-inhibitory casein peptides
description: Bioactive peptides released from casein during cheese fermentation and digestion; inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) — the same target as antihypertensive drugs; identified in cultures of Graviera-native L. plantarum strains

name: Lactobacillus plantarum (native LAB)
description: Probiotic lactic acid bacteria strains isolated directly from traditional Graviera (ACA-DC 2640 and ACA-DC 4039); adhere to human gut epithelial cells; upregulate anti-inflammatory IL-10; produce ACE-inhibitory metabolites in cell-based studies

name: Thymol
description: Phenolic monoterpene derived from Thymus plant nectar; primary marker compound of thyme honey; disrupts bacterial cell membrane integrity and inhibits biofilm formation (S. aureus inhibition up to 80%); key driver of thyme honey's antimicrobial activity and exceptionally high total phenolic content (up to 193 mg/100g — among the highest recorded for any honey variety)

name: Kaempferol
description: Flavonol polyphenol transferred into honey from Thymus plant origin; anti-inflammatory and antioxidant; contributes to thyme honey's mucosal-protective properties and high DPPH radical-scavenging capacity (IC50 15.37 mg/mL)

name: Cichoric acid
description: Primary phenolic acid of Cichorium spinosum (dicaffeoyl tartaric acid); strongest antioxidant compound in traditional stamnagathi decoctions; significantly reduces intracellular ROS in human cells; DPPH IC50 ~15 μg/mL; the defining phytochemical marker of the Cretan stamnagathi decoction

name: Caftaric acid
description: Second major phenolic acid in stamnagathi decoctions (caffeoyl tartaric acid); strong free-radical scavenging activity; identified alongside cichoric acid as a primary antioxidant in Cretan C. spinosum; contributes to the vascular-protective polyphenol profile

name: 8-Deacetylmatricarin-8-O-sulphate (Cretan sesquiterpene lactone)
description: Sulfoconjugate sesquiterpene lactone isolated exclusively from Cretan Cichorium spinosum — not found in C. intybus or other chicory varieties; represents a chemotaxonomic marker unique to the Cretan species; class of sesquiterpene lactones (including lactupicrin) associated with anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective biological activity

name: Carvacrol
description: Phenolic monoterpene comprising 52.2% of dittany essential oil; primary antimicrobial driver — disrupts bacterial cell membranes against S. aureus, E. coli, Listeria, and Salmonella; potent DPPH antioxidant (IC50 0.045% v/v); responsible for the characteristic warm, spicy aroma; also inhibits acetylcholinesterase and interacts with alpha-glucosidase active site (molecular docking)

name: Rosmarinic acid
description: Major polyphenolic ester in dittany polar extracts; strong anti-inflammatory and antioxidant; inhibits COX enzymes and NF-kB pathways; dominant polar phenolic alongside the novel benzodioxane depside salvianolic acid P (first isolated from dittany)

name: Apigenin
description: Flavonoid isolated from dittany; inhibits acetylcholinesterase (AChE) in vitro — an enzyme whose excess activity is associated with Alzheimer's disease; anti-inflammatory and antioxidant

name: Novel luteolin/apigenin glycosides
description: Four novel flavone glycosides described for the first time in O. dictamnus infusion (Paloukopoulou 2026) including luteolin-7-O-[caffeoylglucuronyl]-glucuronopyranoside; structurally unique to dittany; contribute to the spasmolytic gut motility activity observed in ex vivo intestinal model

name: Galactomannans (locust bean gum)
description: Soluble dietary fibre comprising ~75% of carob seed endosperm; viscous in solution — slows gastric emptying and cholesterol absorption; fermented by gut bacteria to produce short-chain fatty acids; responsible for the satiety and glycaemic-moderating effects of carob

name: D-pinitol
description: Unique cyclitol compound (3-O-methyl-D-chiro-inositol) abundant in carob pulp; acts as an insulin sensitiser — enhances glucose uptake into cells via insulin-independent pathways; one of the proposed mechanisms for carob's ability to reduce postprandial glucose response and support metabolic health

name: Condensed tannins (proanthocyanidins)
description: Polyphenolic compounds responsible for carob's cholesterol-lowering effects; bind bile acids in the gut, reducing their reabsorption and forcing the liver to convert more LDL cholesterol into bile acids — the same mechanism as cholestyramine; also antioxidant and anti-inflammatory

name: Quercetin and myricetin
description: Flavonol polyphenols in carob pods and leaves; antioxidant and cardioprotective; contribute to carob's overall polyphenol content alongside gallic acid and ellagic acid

name: Punicalagins
description: Largest-molecular-weight ellagitannins found in pomegranate peel and juice; hydrolysed in the gut to ellagic acid then metabolised by gut bacteria to urolithins; responsible for pomegranate's exceptional antioxidant capacity — demonstrated to exceed both red wine and green tea by standardised ORAC assay; the key compounds driving anti-inflammatory and vascular effects observed in clinical trials

name: Anthocyanins (delphinidin
description: cyanidin
column6: Polyphenolic pigments concentrated in pomegranate arils and juice; produce the characteristic deep red colour; anti-inflammatory via NF-κB pathway suppression; inhibit ICAM-1 and IL-6 expression — matching the biomarkers improved in the 2025 meta-analysis of 19 clinical trials; also antioxidant and cardioprotective

name: Punicic acid (Omega-5 fatty acid)
description: Unusual conjugated linolenic acid (18:3 cis-9 trans-11 cis-13) present in pomegranate seed oil; a structural isomer of conjugated linolenic acid; anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative properties; acts via PPAR-gamma activation to modulate lipid metabolism

name: Cynarin (1
description: 5-dicaffeoylquinic acid)
column5: The signature bitter phenolic of artichoke; directly stimulates bile secretion from the liver and gallbladder; bile acid export lowers hepatic cholesterol pools — the mechanism by which artichoke leaf extract reduces LDL in humans; responsible for the distinctive flavour and the post-artichoke sweet-water perception

name: Chlorogenic acid
description: Hydroxycinnamic acid polyphenol abundant in artichoke leaves and bracts; antioxidant and anti-inflammatory; inhibits glucose-6-phosphatase in the liver — reduces hepatic glucose output; also found in high concentrations in green coffee

name: Inulin (fructooligosaccharides)
description: Prebiotic soluble fibre comprising the storage carbohydrate of artichoke; selectively feeds Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus species; fermented to butyrate and SCFAs in the colon; improves bowel transit and supports the gut epithelial barrier

name: Oleuropein
description: The dominant bitter secoiridoid glycoside in olive leaves; present at 60-90 mg/g dry leaf weight — 10-20x higher than in olive oil; ACE-inhibitory activity lowers blood pressure; antioxidant; hydrolysed in the body to hydroxytyrosol and elenolic acid; the primary compound responsible for antihypertensive effects demonstrated in human crossover RCTs

name: Hydroxytyrosol
description: One of the most potent plant-derived antioxidants known; anti-inflammatory via NF-κB and COX-2 suppression; found in olive leaves at higher concentrations than in EVOO; metabolite of oleuropein; contributes to lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory effects of olive leaf extract observed in clinical trials

name: Beta-glucan (barley)
description: Viscous soluble dietary fibre comprising 3-11% of whole-grain barley by weight; forms a thick gel in the small intestine that traps bile acids, preventing their reabsorption and forcing the liver to convert LDL cholesterol into replacement bile acids; this mechanism earned an FDA-approved cardiovascular health claim; a 50g serving of Cretan paximadi provides approximately 2-3g beta-glucan

name: Arabinoxylan
description: Insoluble prebiotic fibre comprising the cell walls of barley bran; fermented by colonic bacteria to produce butyrate, propionate, and acetate; butyrate is the preferred energy substrate of colonocytes; supports colon health, reduces intestinal inflammation, and improves insulin sensitivity via SCFA signalling

name: Allicin (diallyl thiosulfinate)
description: The primary bioactive compound in garlic; produced when garlic cells are broken — the enzyme alliinase converts inactive alliin into allicin; inhibits HMG-CoA reductase (the same enzyme targeted by statin cholesterol-lowering drugs); inhibits platelet aggregation; potent antimicrobial; half-life ~6 hours in the body — freshly crushed raw garlic delivers the highest allicin dose

name: Organosulfur compounds (S-allylcysteine
description: ajoene
column6: The broader family of stable sulfur compounds to which allicin degrades; S-allylcysteine is the primary compound in aged garlic extract and is highly bioavailable; antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antiplatelet; ajoene inhibits both platelet aggregation and HMG-CoA reductase; responsible for the sustained cardiovascular effects seen in aged garlic RCTs

name: Alliin
description: The inactive odourless precursor compound stored in intact garlic cloves; structurally a cysteine sulphoxide; rapidly converted to allicin by the enzyme alliinase when cell walls are disrupted by chopping, crushing, or chewing; the reason whole uncut garlic has minimal biological activity but crushed garlic has potent effects

name: Monounsaturated fatty acids (oleic acid
description: palmitoleic acid)
column5: Comprise approximately 70% of avocado's total fat content; oleic acid is the same fatty acid that dominates EVOO; substituting saturated dietary fat with MUFA reduces LDL cholesterol without reducing HDL; palmitoleic acid has additional anti-inflammatory properties; the high MUFA content accounts for the cardiovascular benefits seen in avocado RCTs

name: Beta-sitosterol
description: The dominant plant sterol in avocado; structurally similar to cholesterol and competitively inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption by displacing cholesterol from bile acid micelles; avocado contains more beta-sitosterol than any other commonly consumed fruit; FDA recognises plant sterols as having a cardiovascular health claim at 0.8g/day — a typical avocado provides approximately 0.1g

name: Lutein and zeaxanthin
description: Carotenoid antioxidants accumulated preferentially in the macula of the eye; avocado is one of the few fruits (rather than green vegetables) that contains meaningful quantities; associated in prospective cohort studies with reduced risk of age-related macular degeneration and cataracts; also antioxidant in cardiovascular tissues

name: Hydroxytyrosol (free form)
description: The primary phenolic antioxidant in table olives present at 8-fold higher concentration per gram than in extra virgin olive oil; the fermentation and curing process hydrolyses oleuropein glucoside into free hydroxytyrosol; demonstrated to be bioavailable in humans — plasma levels peak within 30 minutes of olive consumption; inhibits LDL oxidation, platelet aggregation, and endothelial inflammation via NF-κB; the same compound responsible for the cardiovascular benefits documented in the PREDIMED trial

name: Oleuropein glucoside and its aglycone
description: The intact precursor compound of hydroxytyrosol present in fresh uncured olives; provides characteristic extreme bitterness of raw olives before curing; the curing process hydrolyses the glucoside bond and further breaks down oleuropein aglycone to release free hydroxytyrosol and elenolic acid; different curing methods (brine vs dry salt vs lye) produce different polyphenol profiles; naturally cured Greek-style olives retain higher total polyphenol content than commercially processed varieties

name: Tyrosol
description: Secondary olive phenolic co-occurring with hydroxytyrosol throughout the Olea europaea plant; weaker antioxidant than HT but present at significant quantities in both olive oil and table olives; both HT and tyrosol are consistently detectable in human plasma after olive consumption in pharmacokinetic studies; anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet activity in vitro; contributes additively to the overall phenolic protection of the olive polyphenol matrix

name: Lactobacillus acidophilus and L. bulgaricus (live cultures)
description: The active therapeutic agents in traditionally fermented yoghurt; L. acidophilus produces bile salt hydrolase (BSH) — the enzyme that deconjugates bile acids in the gut, forcing the liver to synthesise replacement bile acids from circulating LDL cholesterol, directly lowering LDL; L. bulgaricus produces lactic acid and bacteriocins; both strains survive gastric transit in yoghurt matrix better than in capsule form; the live probiotic count at consumption is the primary determinant of cholesterol-lowering efficacy

name: Casein-derived ACE-inhibitory peptides (Val-Pro-Pro; Ile-Pro-Pro)
description: Bioactive tripeptides released during fermentation of sheep and goat casein by lactic acid bacteria; competitively inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) — the same enzyme targeted by prescription ACE-inhibitor antihypertensive drugs (ramipril, lisinopril); blood pressure reduction from fermented dairy consumption in human trials is partially attributed to these peptides; sheep and goat milk casein yields higher ACE-inhibitory peptide concentrations than cow casein due to different protein composition

name: Carvacrol
description: The dominant phenolic monoterpenoid in Satureja thymbra essential oil (40-70% of oil); identical compound to the primary bioactive in Origanum and other Cretan medicinal herbs; the active agent responsible for the metabolic effects seen in the Satureja khuzestanica RCT (FBS reduction, HbA1c improvement, lipid normalisation); inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) reducing prostaglandin synthesis; strong antimicrobial membrane disruptor active against MRSA and enteric pathogens

name: Rosmarinic acid
description: Polyphenol ester abundant in all Lamiaceae family herbs including savory, oregano, dittany, rosemary, and basil; potent antioxidant with ORAC value exceeding vitamin C; inhibits complement system C3 convertase activation and 5-lipoxygenase, reducing both inflammatory cascade activation and leukotriene synthesis; well-studied in in vitro models; European Medicines Agency has accepted rosmarinic acid content as a quality marker for medicinal Lamiaceae herbs

name: Thymol
description: Phenolic monoterpenoid co-occurring with carvacrol; same compound dominant in thyme; antimicrobial membrane disruptor particularly effective against biofilm-forming bacteria; exhibits HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity in mechanistic studies (same molecular target as statin drugs); the combination of carvacrol and thymol shows synergistic antimicrobial activity greater than either compound alone — the natural ratio in Satureja essential oil is likely more effective than isolated compounds

name: Lycopene
description: The dominant carotenoid giving tomatoes their red colour; fat-soluble and dramatically more bioavailable from cooked processed tomatoes than raw — the traditional Cretan preparation of slow-cooked tomato sauce with EVOO is optimal for lycopene extraction; inhibits LDL oxidation, reduces endothelial cell adhesion molecule expression, and lowers systolic blood pressure via NO pathway enhancement; meta-analysis of ≥25mg/day doses: LDL −10.35 mg/dL and SBP −5.60 mmHg; Crete's sun-grown tomatoes have higher lycopene than northern European varieties

name: Chlorogenic acid
description: The primary polyphenol in tomatoes and one of the most abundant dietary polyphenols globally; inhibits glucose-6-phosphatase (enzyme that releases glucose into the bloodstream from glycogen stores), contributing to fasting blood glucose reduction; the same compound that accounts for much of the cardiovascular benefit of coffee consumption; ACE-inhibitory activity contributes to blood pressure reduction; significant antioxidant activity and NF-κB suppression

name: Beta-carotene and full carotenoid family (phytoene; phytofluene; lutein)
description: Tomatoes provide the complete carotenoid family, not just lycopene; beta-carotene is provitamin A; phytoene and phytofluene are UV-absorbing carotenoids with documented skin photoprotection; lutein accumulates in the macula of the eye; the full carotenoid matrix from whole tomatoes shows stronger protective effects in prospective studies than isolated lycopene supplementation, suggesting synergistic activity — consistent with traditional whole-food consumption patterns

name: Quercetin and isorhamnetin
description: The dominant flavonols in onions; quercetin is one of the most extensively studied dietary polyphenols across all food science; in onions it occurs primarily as quercetin glucoside (quercetin-4'-O-glucoside), hydrolysed by the small intestinal enzyme LPH giving unusually high bioavailability; inhibits ACE (blood pressure reduction), HMG-CoA reductase (cholesterol lowering), and platelet thromboxane A2 synthesis (antiplatelet); onion skin provides 3-4x higher quercetin concentration than edible flesh — outer brown and red layers most concentrated

name: Organosulfur compounds (propanethial S-oxide; dipropyl disulfide)
description: The volatile lachrymatory factor released when onions are cut; distinct from garlic's alliin/allicin pathway — onion produces propanethial S-oxide rather than allicin; demonstrates antiplatelet activity by inhibiting thromboxane B2 synthesis and platelet aggregation in vitro; dipropyl disulfide shows antimicrobial and antifungal properties; traditional attribution of onions as a natural blood thinner is mechanistically supported by these sulfur compounds, though human clinical evidence is less robust than for quercetin

name: Carvacrol
description: The dominant phenolic monoterpenoid in Origanum vulgare essential oil, comprising 60-80% of Cretan wild oregano oil; Greek wild oregano contains among the highest carvacrol concentrations documented globally — Cretan rigani is prized partly for this potency; identical bioactive compound found in Cretan dittany and savory; inhibits COX-1, COX-2, NF-κB, and LPS-induced cytokine release; potent broad-spectrum antimicrobial disrupting bacterial cell membrane integrity; EFSA has noted carvacrol as a flavouring with documented biological activity

name: Rosmarinic acid
description: Polyphenol ester at 10-20 mg/g dry weight in Origanum vulgare — higher than in rosemary despite the name; potent antioxidant (3x more potent than vitamin C by DPPH assay); inhibits complement C3 convertase activation and 5-lipoxygenase, reducing both complement-mediated and leukotriene-mediated inflammation; European Medicines Agency uses rosmarinic acid content as a quality marker for medicinal Lamiaceae preparations; anti-inflammatory mechanism relevant to atherosclerosis, arthritis, and neuroinflammation

name: Acetic acid
description: The primary bioactive in all vinegars (4-8% w/v); mechanism: acetic acid is absorbed in the small intestine and activates AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) — the same energy-sensing enzyme activated by the diabetes drug metformin — suppressing hepatic glucose production and increasing peripheral glucose uptake; slows gastric emptying, reducing the rate of carbohydrate digestion and postprandial glucose spikes; meta-analysis of 9 RCTs: FPG −7.97 mg/dL, HbA1c −0.50, TC −6.06 mg/dL; effects on TC likely via AMPK-mediated HMG-CoA reductase inhibition

name: Grape polyphenols (resveratrol; quercetin; catechins; anthocyanins)
description: Polyphenols from Cretan grape varieties (Vidiano, Vilana, Mandilari) that partially survive the double fermentation process; resveratrol content varies with grape variety and processing but is measurable in wine vinegars from red varieties; quercetin from grape skins contributes antioxidant and ACE-inhibitory activity; catechin content reduces LDL oxidation; Cretan Mandilari (a high-anthocyanin red variety) produces vinegar with higher polyphenol content than most commercial wine vinegars — the full health benefits are additive to the acetic acid effect

name: Trans-anethole
description: The primary volatile compound in fennel essential oil (60-80%); responsible for the characteristic anise flavour; primary spasmolytic agent — relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle by inhibiting calcium-mediated and serotonin-mediated contractions; demonstrated carminative (gas-relieving) activity by reducing intestinal motility and intraluminal pressure; mild estrogenic activity at high doses (relevant to traditional use for menstrual regulation); anti-inflammatory activity via NF-κB suppression; the spasmolytic mechanism explains why both traditional fennel seed tea and the clinical RCT results converge on gut comfort benefits

name: Fenchone and fenchyl alcohol
description: Secondary monoterpenoids contributing 10-20% of fennel essential oil; fenchone has documented expectorant, antimicrobial, and antifungal properties; FAAH (fatty acid amide hydrolase) inhibitory activity — FAAH degrades endocannabinoids, so its inhibition extends endocannabinoid signalling, which contributes to GI motility regulation and pain reduction; fenchyl alcohol demonstrates additional spasmolytic activity synergistic with trans-anethole; the combination of trans-anethole and fenchone in whole fennel oil is more effective than isolated anethole, consistent with whole-herb traditional use

name: Melatonin
description: Tomatoes contain dietary melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) — the same hormone the pineal gland releases at night to signal sleep onset; plants synthesise melatonin from tryptophan via the same enzymatic pathway as mammals (tryptophan → serotonin → N-acetylserotonin → melatonin); beefsteak tomato has the highest melatonin content of common tomato varieties tested; when consumed 2 h before sleep at a 250 g portion, raises urinary 6-sulphatoxymelatonin (the primary melatonin metabolite) approximately 10-fold; melatonin is also a potent direct free-radical scavenger and mitochondrial antioxidant, complementing the carotenoid antioxidant system already present in the fruit; concentrations are well below pharmacological supplement doses (0.5–5 mg), but the Cretan tradition of slow-cooked evening tomato dishes may incidentally support circadian melatonin signalling

name: Masticadienonic acid
description: Pentacyclic triterpenic acid characteristic of Pistacia lentiscus var. chia (Chios mastic); one of the dominant bioactive triterpenoids in mastic gum responsible for the documented effects on gastrointestinal motility and mucosal protection; mechanism: inhibits gastric H+/K+-ATPase activity and modulates intestinal smooth muscle contractility; serves as a chemotaxonomic marker for authentic Chios-variant mastic

name: Isomasticadienonic acid
description: Isomer of masticadienonic acid co-occurring in Pistacia lentiscus resin; contributes to the overall triterpenoid profile responsible for mastics prokinetic and anti-Helicobacter pylori activity demonstrated in clinical trials; the combination of masticadienonic acid and isomasticadienonic acid distinguishes Chios mastic from other Pistacia lentiscus varieties

name: Alpha-pinene
description: Bicyclic monoterpene comprising 50-80% of mastic essential oil — responsible for the characteristic pine-resinous aroma; potent antimicrobial against oral pathogens (S. mutans, P. gingivalis) and gastric pathogens (H. pylori) at concentrations achieved through mastic consumption; partly volatilises during cooking but is retained in chewed mastic gum and in distilled mastichi liqueur

name: Beta-myrcene and other monoterpenes
description: Volatile monoterpene fraction of mastic essential oil (10-20%); contributes additional antimicrobial activity and may modulate gastrointestinal motility through TRP channel interactions; the whole essential oil matrix appears to be more effective than isolated alpha-pinene alone, suggesting synergistic activity consistent with traditional whole-resin consumption rather than isolated compound supplementation

name: Rutin (quercetin-3-O-rutinoside)
description: Quercetin glycoside present in caper fruit and buds at among the highest concentrations documented in any vegetable food (170-330 mg/100g in fresh capers); rutin is hydrolysed by gut bacteria to quercetin, which inhibits alpha-glucosidase (lowering post-prandial glucose), aldose reductase (reducing diabetic complications), and ACE (lowering blood pressure); rutin specifically also has direct antithrombotic activity and microvascular protective effects

name: Quercetin
description: Aglycone flavonol released from caper rutin by intestinal hydrolysis; one of the most extensively studied dietary polyphenols globally; in capers, quercetin occurs both as the glycoside (rutin) and in free form; inhibits ACE (blood pressure reduction), HMG-CoA reductase (cholesterol lowering), and platelet thromboxane synthesis; quercetin from capers complements the quercetin already provided by Cretan onions and contributes to the overall flavonol load of traditional Cretan cuisine

name: Kaempferol and stachydrine
description: Kaempferol is the second major flavonol in caper (~50-100 mg/100g) with anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet activity; stachydrine is a quaternary ammonium alkaloid unique to capers and a few other Capparidaceae plants that contributes to the bitter-pungent flavour and shows modest anti-inflammatory and cardioprotective activity in animal models; the multi-compound profile of capers makes them one of the more flavonoid-dense vegetables in the Mediterranean diet

name: Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA)
description: Plant omega-3 fatty acid (18:3 n-3) comprising 9-14% of walnut fat — the highest concentration among commonly consumed nuts; the body converts a fraction of ALA to EPA and DHA, providing cardiovascular benefits without consuming fish; ALA itself reduces LDL oxidation, modulates inflammatory cytokine production, and improves endothelial function as measured by flow-mediated dilation; walnut ALA is the primary mechanism behind the documented FMD improvement in pre-diabetic and metabolic syndrome populations

name: Gamma-tocopherol
description: Less famous than alpha-tocopherol but more abundant in walnuts; gamma-tocopherol specifically traps reactive nitrogen species (peroxynitrite) that alpha-tocopherol cannot — a complementary antioxidant activity; walnut contains 5-10x more gamma-tocopherol than most other nuts; serum gamma-tocopherol levels are inversely associated with cardiovascular risk in prospective cohort data; the walnut tocopherol mix is one of the few dietary sources delivering meaningful gamma-tocopherol

name: Ellagic acid and ellagitannins
description: Polyphenols abundant in walnut pellicle (the brown skin); metabolised by gut bacteria to urolithins — the same secondary metabolites produced from pomegranate punicalagins; urolithin A has been shown to activate mitophagy (the cellular recycling of dysfunctional mitochondria) and is associated with improved muscle function in older adults; walnut and pomegranate provide overlapping urolithin precursor pools in the traditional Cretan diet

name: Walnut melatonin
description: Walnuts contain dietary melatonin at 3-4 ng/g — among the higher concentrations in nuts; consuming walnuts has been documented to raise serum melatonin in human pharmacokinetic studies; when combined with the omega-3 content, walnuts deliver both a circadian signal and the neuro-supportive fatty acid substrate; complements the dietary melatonin available from Cretan tomatoes and purslane

name: Alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E)
description: Almonds contain 25-30 mg alpha-tocopherol per 100g — the richest plant source among commonly consumed foods; a 28g portion (one ounce) provides ~7 mg, nearly half the adult RDA; alpha-tocopherol inhibits LDL oxidation, a critical step in atherosclerosis; the skin (brown outer layer) of almonds also contains polyphenols (catechins, epicatechin) that act synergistically with vitamin E to extend the lag phase of LDL oxidation

name: Oleic acid (MUFA)
description: Almond fat is dominated by oleic acid — the same monounsaturated fatty acid that makes olive oil cardiovascular-protective; substituting dietary saturated fat with almond MUFA lowers LDL cholesterol without reducing protective HDL; this is the primary mechanism behind the consistent ~5-10 mg/dL LDL reductions documented across multiple almond meta-analyses; the oleic acid in almonds complements rather than duplicates the oleic acid from olive oil — almonds deliver this MUFA in a fibre + protein matrix that increases satiety

name: Magnesium and prebiotic fibre
description: Almonds provide 270 mg magnesium per 100g — among the highest dietary sources; magnesium is a cofactor for over 300 enzymatic reactions including those regulating blood pressure and insulin signalling; almond fibre (~12g per 100g, mostly insoluble) is fermented by colonic bacteria to short-chain fatty acids and acts as a prebiotic, modulating gut microbiota composition in human trials; the magnesium + fibre + MUFA combination explains the body weight (−1.39 kg) and blood pressure improvements observed in the Lee-Bravatti 2019 meta-analysis

name: Carnosic acid and carnosol
description: Carnosic acid is the dominant diterpene phenolic in Salvia fruticosa and the related Mediterranean sages; oxidises to carnosol in plant tissue and during storage; both compounds are potent antioxidants and crystallographically documented to inhibit acetylcholinesterase (AChE) — the molecular target of prescription Alzheimers drugs (donepezil, rivastigmine); rosemary and sage are the richest dietary sources of carnosic acid; the same mechanism (AChE inhibition) explains the cognitive enhancement documented in the Wightman 2021 RCT and the Miroddi 2014 systematic review
8-Cineole (eucalyptol)
column5: Volatile monoterpenoid comprising 30-60% of Greek sage (Salvia fruticosa) essential oil — the chemotype that distinguishes Cretan faskomilo from Northern European Salvia officinalis (which is dominated by alpha-thujone); 1,8-cineole crosses the blood-brain barrier rapidly and inhibits both AChE and BuChE in vitro; serum 1,8-cineole concentrations correlate with cognitive performance in human pharmacokinetic studies of inhaled and oral eucalyptol exposure

name: Rosmarinic acid
description: Polyphenol ester present at high concentrations in all Mediterranean Lamiaceae herbs — sage, oregano, savory, dittany, rosemary, lemon balm; ORAC antioxidant value exceeding vitamin C; inhibits complement C3 convertase and 5-lipoxygenase, reducing both complement-mediated and leukotriene-mediated inflammation; in faskomilo specifically, rosmarinic acid contributes both to the cognitive support (via brain antioxidant protection) and to the traditional Cretan reputation of sage tea for cleansing the body
